findings.text: The first paragraph tells a newcomer what Athena is, who it is for and what problem it solves. Someone who reads only this paragraph can already say what the project is and why it matters.
findings.source: "Athena is an open-source system, written in Rust, that turns a short request into a change to a code repository. ... It solves the problem of AI edits that arrive unreviewed and unaccountable."

findings.text: The page title and heading name a different project, firstmate. A newcomer who came to Athena's home page may think they have landed on the wrong site until they read the first paragraph.

The first section after the navigation is an error message. It appears exactly where the page should prove what the first paragraph promises: models, verdict and cost. A newcomer sees the main selling point fail before seeing it work.
findings.source: Check it on a real job: "The records of job 20261029-073603-7kqv could not be read here, so no models, verdict or costs are shown: no reading record for job 20261029-073603-7kqv."

findings.text: The header has a link meant for the project owner. A newcomer has no proposals to decide on, so the link is confusing without a note on who it is for.
findings.source: "Owner view: proposals waiting for your decision."

findings.text: The next steps are concrete and in order: prerequisites, clone, install, then a first command with what to expect. The "Next step" link in the header points there, so a newcomer can find what to do next quickly.
findings.source: Next steps: "Before installing, check that you have these prerequisites" ... "Install Athena from the checkout: ./setup.sh" ... "Try it with a one-line request: athena ask \"add a changelog\""

findings.text: Claude Code is listed as a prerequisite, but the page does not say whether it needs an account, an API key or a paid plan, or which operating systems Athena runs on. A newcomer may find this out only partway through setup.
findings.source: Prerequisites: "Claude Code, or npm to install it."

findings.text: The page explains why the firstmate study is shown: it demonstrates Athena's traceable reading of an unfamiliar project. The 45 linked claims back this up. But most of the page is firstmate detail, such as states, transitions and the glossary, which a newcomer who wants to learn about Athena will probably skim past.
findings.source: "A study is Athena's written reading of another software project, taken at one fixed commit ... with every statement traced to a claim, and every claim to lines in the project's own files."

findings.text: Hiding the Counters and Transitions sections behind an expert toggle keeps the default reading shorter. Even so, the default sections are dense, with exit codes, lock behaviour and terms such as "captain call" that the page itself says the source does not define.
findings.source: Learning path: "Show expert detail (core track is the default)"
